(Section: on mention of some of the Torah's good tidings of the Messenger of God ﷺ)

It is said in the Torah in the Fifth Book: "God came from Sinai, and was manifest from Seir, and appeared from the mountains of Paran, and with Him were ten thousands of holy ones at His right hand." This contains the three prophethoods: the prophethood of Moses, the prophethood of Jesus, and the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ.

His coming from Sinai, which is the mountain on which God spoke to Moses and gave him tidings, is an announcement of his prophethood.

His manifestation from Seir is the manifestation of Jesus the Messiah from Bayt al-Maqdis. Seir is a well-known village there to this day, and this is a good tiding of the prophethood of the Messiah.

Paran is Mecca. God, glory be to Him and exalted, likened the prophethood of Moses to the coming of dawn and its breaking, the prophethood of the Messiah after it to its shining and light, and the prophethood of the Seal of the Prophets after both of them ﷺ to the sun's rising, its appearing, and the appearing of its light on the horizons. The matter occurred exactly as He had announced. God split the darkness of disbelief with the prophethood of Moses and lit its dawn with his prophethood; the light and brightness increased with the prophethood of the Messiah; and the light was perfected, became manifest, and covered the earth with the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ.

The mention of these three prophethoods contained in this good tiding is like their mention at the beginning of the surah: ﴿By the fig and the olive, and Mount Sinai, and this secure city.﴾

So He mentioned the places of these prophets and the lands from which they went forth. "The fig and the olive" means their place of growth and their land, which is the holy land that is the manifestation of the Messiah. "Mount Sinai" is the mountain on which God spoke to Moses, and it is the manifestation of his prophethood. "This secure city" is Mecca, the sanctuary and safety of God, which is the manifestation of the prophethood of Muhammad, may the blessings and peace of God be upon him and upon them all.

These three are exactly parallel to those three.

The Jews said: Paran is the land of Syria and not the land of the Hijaz. This is no novelty from their deceit and distortion. They have in the Torah that when Ishmael separated from his father he dwelt in the wilderness of Paran; thus the Torah speaks, and its wording is: "And Ishmael dwelt in the wilderness of Paran, and his mother took for him a wife from the land of Egypt."

The scholars of the People of the Book do not doubt that Paran is the dwelling of the family of Ishmael. The Torah contains a prophethood that would descend in the land of Paran, and contains a prophethood that would descend upon a great one of the offspring of Ishmael, and contains the spread of his nation and followers until they fill the plain and the mountain, as we shall mention, God willing.

After this there remains no doubt at all that this is the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ, which descended in Paran upon the most noble of the offspring of Ishmael, until he filled the earth with light and radiance, and his followers filled the plain and the mountain. It is not strange that among the people whom the Torah describes as lacking judgment and understanding there should be a division into the ignorant of this, and the obstinate, arrogant denier.

The wording of the Torah concerning them is: that they are a people lacking judgment, and there is no understanding in them.

It is said to these arrogant deniers: What prophethood came out of Syria and shone forth like the light of the sun, and appeared above the two prophethoods before it?! Is this anything but like the stubbornness of one who sees the sun rise from the east, yet deceives, is arrogant, and says, "Rather, it rose from the west"?

It is said in the Torah in the First Book: "The angel appeared to Hagar, the mother of Ishmael, and said: O Hagar, where have you come from, and where are you going? When she explained her situation to him, he said: Return, for I will greatly multiply your descendants and your offspring until they cannot be counted for multitude. Behold, you will conceive and bear a son whose name is Ishmael, because God has heard your humbling and your submission. Your son will be a wild man of the people, his hand will be over all, and the hand of all will be stretched out to him in submission."

This is a good tiding containing that his son's hand would be over the hand of all creatures, that his word would be exalted, that his hand would be high, and that the hand of creation would be beneath his hand. Who, then, is it that this description fits except Muhammad son of Abd Allah, may the blessings and peace of God be upon him?

Likewise, in the First Book of the Torah: God said to Abraham: "Indeed I will make your son Ishmael a great nation, since he is of your seed."

This is a good tiding of one who would be made of his offspring into a great nation, and it is none other than Muhammad son of Abd Allah ﷺ.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 95, verse 4:

Since the predominant mode of the Children of Israel was judgment by the senses (hukm al-hiss), He mentioned that in conformity with reality. Since the predominant mode of the complete community was judgment by the intellect (hukm al-'aql), He mentioned them in intellectual order, and He swore by them at the beginning and the end of the human being, and said: ﴿Indeed, We created man in the best of stature.﴾

That is, in the finest form, shape and proportion, upright of stature, balanced in creation, complete in fashion, better than every other animal. Taqwim (proper formation, "stature") means placing a thing in the state it ought to be in its composition and arrangement. This was His handiwork, blessed and exalted, in a handful of earth, and by observation He created him from a drop of water. This is among the greatest signs indicating His existence, power, wisdom, knowledge and attributes of perfection. For this reason He repeats it often in the Qur'an, because of the lesson it contains and because it is the closest route to reasoning about His oneness, the origin (mabda') and the return (ma'ad).

His oath by these three places, which indicate Him and His knowledge and wisdom, includes His care for His creation, in that He sent from among them messengers, to whom He revealed His books, to make the servants know their Lord and His rights over them, to warn them of God and His vengeance, and to invite them to His honor and reward.

(Admonition)

O you who are among the masters of experience, have you come to know the worth of your self? All the worlds were created only for you.

O you who were nourished with the milk of kindness, and whose heart the hands of gentle kindness have shaped, every thing is a tree, and you are its fruit.

You are the form, and you are the meaning; you are the shell, and you are the pearl; you are the churned milk, and you are the butter.

The manifesto of Our choosing you is clear in its script, but your extraction (of its meaning) is weak.

Whenever you seek Me, seek Me in yourself; seek Me from yourself and you will find Me near. Do not seek Me from other than you, for I am closer to you than that.

If you knew the measure of your self in Our sight, you would not humiliate it with sins. We only expelled Iblis when he did not prostrate to you while you were in your father's loins. So how strange! How could you make peace with him and abandon Us?!

Then, since people are of two groups in responding to this call, some answering and some refusing, He mentioned the condition of both groups. He mentioned the condition of the majority, who are "returned to the lowest of the low" (asfal safilin). The correct view is that this is the Fire, as said by Mujahid, al-Hasan and Abu al-'Aliyah.

Ali ibn Abi Talib (raḍiyallahu ʿanhu) said: it is the Fire, some of it lower than other parts.

A group, including Qatadah, Ikrimah, ʿAta', al-Kalbi and Ibrahim, said that it is "the most abject age" (arhal al-ʿumr).

This is also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The correct view is the first opinion, for several reasons:

First, arhal al-ʿumr is not called asfal safilin, neither linguistically nor by common usage. Rather, asfal safilin is Sijjin, which is the place of the wicked, just as ʿIlliyyin is the place of the righteous.

Second, those returned to the lowest age, relative to mankind as a whole, are very few. Most of them die and are not returned to the most abject age.

Third, those who believed and did righteous deeds are equal to others in being returned to the most abject age if their lives are prolonged. So this is not specific to disbelievers, such that believers would need to be excepted from it.

Fourth, when Allah, glorified is He, willed this, He did not restrict it to disbelievers but made it for the whole human species. He said: ﴿And among you is he who is taken in death, and among you is he who is returned to the most abject age, so that he knows nothing after knowledge.﴾

So He made them two categories: one category taken in death before old age, and one category returned to the most abject age. He did not call it asfal safilin.

Fifth, the contrast between the most abject age and the reward of the believers is not fitting, whereas Allah, glorified is He, contrasted the recompense of these people with the recompense of the people of faith. He made the recompense of the disbelievers asfal safilin and the recompense of the believers "a reward never cut off" (ajran ghayra mamnun).

Sixth, the view of those who explained it as the most abject age entails that the verse is empty of the recompense of the disbelievers and the outcome of their affair. It also entails explaining it by something perceptible, so that the most important meaning is left aside and the verse speaks of a matter known through the senses and observation. In that there is a diminishing of the meaning of the verse and a falling short of the meaning appropriate to it.

Seventh, He, glorified is He, mentioned the condition of man at his beginning and his return. His beginning is his creation "in the best of forms," and his return is his being sent back to asfal safilin or to a reward never cut off.

This agrees with the method and custom of the Qur'an in mentioning the beginning and return of the servant, whereas "the most abject age" does not fit this.

This is the meaning intended, the one to be established and argued for.

Eighth, the proponents of the first view are compelled to contradict the senses, to remove the speech from its apparent meaning, and to make a distant strained interpretation. If they say that those returned to the most abject age are the disbelievers and not the believers, they deny what is perceived. If they say that both categories include those returned to the most abject age, they need strained interpretation to make the exception valid. Some of them estimated that the believers who did righteous deeds, when returned to the most abject age, do not have their deeds nullified, but the deeds they used to do in health continue to be recorded for them. This, though true, makes the exception apply only to the return, not to the reward and the deeds. When the proponents of this view realised the strain in it, some of them restricted the believers who did righteous deeds to the recitation of the Qur'an alone, saying that whoever recites the Qur'an is not returned to the most abject age.

This is weak for two reasons:

One, the exception is general for believers, both those who recite and those who are unlettered, and there is no evidence for what they claim.

Two, this is not known through the senses, nor is there any report that must be accepted which requires it. And Allah knows best.

Ninth, He, glorified is He, mentioned His blessing upon man in creating him in the best of forms. This blessing requires him to thank it by faith and by worshipping Him alone, without partner. Then He transfers him from this abode to the highest of ʿIlliyyin. But if he does not believe, associates others with Him and disobeys His messengers, He transfers him from it to asfal safilin and exchanges that form, which was in the best of forms, for one of the most hideous forms in asfal safilin. This is His blessing upon him, and this is His justice regarding him, and His punishment for his ingratitude for the blessing.

Tenth, the parallel of this verse is His saying: ﴿So give them tidings of a painful punishment, except those who believed and did righteous deeds, for them is a reward never cut off.﴾

So the painful punishment is asfal safilin, the excepted ones here are the excepted ones there, and the reward never cut off there is what is mentioned here. And Allah knows best.

As for His saying "ghayra mamnun," it means not cut off, not diminished, and not troubled for them. This is the correct view. Another group said it means "not bestowing a favour upon them," but rather it is the recompense of their deeds. This is narrated from Ikrimah and Muqatil, and it is the view of many of the Qadariyyah. These people said that bestowing a favour spoils the blessing, so the perfection of a blessing is that the giver does not bestow favour on the one who receives it. This view is definitely wrong. Its proponents have likened Allah's blessing upon His servant to a created being's bestowal upon another created being. This is among the most false of falsehoods. The favour that spoils a blessing is the favour of the created upon the created. But the favour of the Creator upon the created is the perfection of the blessing, its sweetness and goodness, for it is a true favour. Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿They consider it a favour to you that they have embraced Islam. Say: Do not consider your Islam a favour to me. Rather, Allah bestows a favour upon you that He guided you to faith, if you are truthful.﴾

And He, the Exalted, says: ﴿And We indeed bestowed favour upon Musa and Harun, and saved them and their people from the great distress.﴾

So it is a favour upon them in the blessing of this world, not in the blessing of the Hereafter.

He said to Musa: ﴿And We bestowed favour upon you another time.﴾

And the people of Paradise said: ﴿So Allah has favoured us and protected us from the punishment of the scorching wind.﴾

And He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Allah certainly bestowed favour upon the believers when He sent among them a messenger from themselves.﴾ and the verse continues.

And He said: ﴿And We wish to bestow favour upon those who were oppressed in the land.﴾ and the verse continues.

In the authentic report, the Prophet (ﷺ) said to the Ansar:

"Did I not find you astray, and Allah guided you through me? Did I not find you poor, and Allah made you rich through me?" Whenever he said something, they would say: "Allah and His Messenger are the most bountiful in favour."

This is the response of those who know Allah and His Messenger. Is the favour, all of it, not for Allah alone, the Bestower of favour by His grace, upon whose favour all creation depends? The favour of the created is only abhorrent because it is a favour with what is not his own, and it is a favour that hurts the one upon whom it is bestowed. But the favour of the Bestower by His grace, without which life is not pleasant, and every blessing from Him in this world and the Hereafter, is a favour He bestows upon the one He has blessed. Such a favour cannot be negated. How can it be said that Allah has no favour upon those who believed and did righteous deeds in entering Paradise? Is this not among the most false of falsehoods?

If it is said: this matter is not hidden from the scholars who said this, and their intention was not what has been mentioned. Rather, their intention was that He does not bestow favour upon them by it, even though the favour is Allah's upon them. He does not bestow favour upon them by it, but it is said: "This is the recompense of your deeds which you did in the world, and this is your reward." You receive the full wages of your deeds; We do not bestow favour upon you with what We have given you.

It is said in reply: this too is the very falsehood itself. That reward is not a price for the deeds, nor an exchange for them. The one most knowledgeable of creation about Allah has said:

"None of you will enter Paradise by his deeds." They said: "Not even you, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Not even I, unless Allah covers me with His mercy and grace."

(Sahih)

So he informed that entry into Paradise is by the mercy and grace of Allah, and that is pure favour from Him upon him and upon all His servants. Just as He, glorified is He, bestows favour by sending His messengers, by granting success in obeying Him, and by helping in it, so He bestows favour by giving the reward. All of this is pure favour, grace and generosity from Him, and no one has a right over Him such that when He fulfils it to him, he would have a favour upon Him. If the view is false in this world, it has nothing to do with Him.

If it is said: how do you say this when He has informed His Messenger that the right of the servants upon Him, if they affirm His oneness, is that He will not punish them, and He has informed about Himself that it is a right upon Himself: "And it is incumbent upon Us to help the believers"?

It is said: by the life of Allah, this is among the greatest of His favours upon His servants, that He made it a right upon Himself by the judgement of His promise, which is true, that He will reward them and not punish them when they worship Him and affirm His oneness. This is part of the perfection of His favour, for if He punished the inhabitants of His heavens and earth, He would punish them and He would not be unjust to them. But His favour required that He make binding upon Himself the reward of those who worship Him and the answering of those who ask Him:

"Nothing is due to the servants from Him as an obligation; nor is anything they strive for lost with Him.
If He punishes them, it is after His justice; or if He blesses them, it is by His grace, for He is the Generous, the Vast."

Then, since people are of two groups in responding to this call, some answering and some refusing, He mentioned the condition of both groups. He mentioned the condition of the majority, who are "returned to the lowest of the low" (asfal safilin). The correct view is that this is the Fire, as said by Mujahid, al-Hasan and Abu al-'Aliyah.

Ali ibn Abi Talib (raḍiyallahu ʿanhu) said: it is the Fire, some of it lower than other parts.

A group, including Qatadah, Ikrimah, ʿAta', al-Kalbi and Ibrahim, said that it is "the most abject age" (arhal al-ʿumr).

This is also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The correct view is the first opinion, for several reasons:

First, arhal al-ʿumr is not called asfal safilin, neither linguistically nor by common usage. Rather, asfal safilin is Sijjin, which is the place of the wicked, just as ʿIlliyyin is the place of the righteous.

Second, those returned to the lowest age, relative to mankind as a whole, are very few. Most of them die and are not returned to the most abject age.

Third, those who believed and did righteous deeds are equal to others in being returned to the most abject age if their lives are prolonged. So this is not specific to disbelievers, such that believers would need to be excepted from it.

Fourth, when Allah, glorified is He, willed this, He did not restrict it to disbelievers but made it for the whole human species. He said: ﴿And among you is he who is taken in death, and among you is he who is returned to the most abject age, so that he knows nothing after knowledge.﴾

So He made them two categories: one category taken in death before old age, and one category returned to the most abject age. He did not call it asfal safilin.

Fifth, the contrast between the most abject age and the reward of the believers is not fitting, whereas Allah, glorified is He, contrasted the recompense of these people with the recompense of the people of faith. He made the recompense of the disbelievers asfal safilin and the recompense of the believers "a reward never cut off" (ajran ghayra mamnun).

Sixth, the view of those who explained it as the most abject age entails that the verse is empty of the recompense of the disbelievers and the outcome of their affair. It also entails explaining it by something perceptible, so that the most important meaning is left aside and the verse speaks of a matter known through the senses and observation. In that there is a diminishing of the meaning of the verse and a falling short of the meaning appropriate to it.

Seventh, He, glorified is He, mentioned the condition of man at his beginning and his return. His beginning is his creation "in the best of forms," and his return is his being sent back to asfal safilin or to a reward never cut off.

This agrees with the method and custom of the Qur'an in mentioning the beginning and return of the servant, whereas "the most abject age" does not fit this.

This is the meaning intended, the one to be established and argued for.

Eighth, the proponents of the first view are compelled to contradict the senses, to remove the speech from its apparent meaning, and to make a distant strained interpretation. If they say that those returned to the most abject age are the disbelievers and not the believers, they deny what is perceived. If they say that both categories include those returned to the most abject age, they need strained interpretation to make the exception valid. Some of them estimated that the believers who did righteous deeds, when returned to the most abject age, do not have their deeds nullified, but the deeds they used to do in health continue to be recorded for them. This, though true, makes the exception apply only to the return, not to the reward and the deeds. When the proponents of this view realised the strain in it, some of them restricted the believers who did righteous deeds to the recitation of the Qur'an alone, saying that whoever recites the Qur'an is not returned to the most abject age.

This is weak for two reasons:

One, the exception is general for believers, both those who recite and those who are unlettered, and there is no evidence for what they claim.

Two, this is not known through the senses, nor is there any report that must be accepted which requires it. And Allah knows best.

Ninth, He, glorified is He, mentioned His blessing upon man in creating him in the best of forms. This blessing requires him to thank it by faith and by worshipping Him alone, without partner. Then He transfers him from this abode to the highest of ʿIlliyyin. But if he does not believe, associates others with Him and disobeys His messengers, He transfers him from it to asfal safilin and exchanges that form, which was in the best of forms, for one of the most hideous forms in asfal safilin. This is His blessing upon him, and this is His justice regarding him, and His punishment for his ingratitude for the blessing.

So the painful punishment is asfal safilin, the excepted ones here are the excepted ones there, and the reward never cut off there is what is mentioned here. And Allah knows best.

This is narrated from Ikrimah and Muqatil, and it is the view of many of the Qadariyyah. Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 95, verses 7–8:

Regarding His words, glorified is He, ﴿So what causes you to deny the Judgment after this?﴾

The more correct of the two opinions is that this is addressed to the human being: that is, "What causes you to deny the recompense and the return after this clarification and this proof? You say that you will not be resurrected or called to account. Yet if you reflected on the beginning of your creation and your form, you would know that the One who created you is more able to restore you after your death and bring you into a new creation. Were that beyond His capacity, the first creation would have been beyond His capacity and would have wearied Him. Moreover, the One who perfected your creation in the best form, after you were a drop of despised fluid, how could it befit Him to leave you neglected, not completing that through command and prohibition, and through making clear what benefits and harms you, and not transferring you to an abode more perfect than this one, making this abode a path for you to it? The wisdom of the Most Wise of judges refuses that and decrees the opposite." Mansur said: I said to Mujahid, "﴿So what causes you to deny the Judgment after this?﴾ is meant to refer to Muhammad," and he said, "God forbid! It is meant only to refer to the human being."

Qatada said the pronoun refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), and al-Farra' chose this view. This is a point that requires explanation and clarification.

It is said: "The man lied (kadhaba al-rajul)" when he spoke falsehood, and "I denied him (kadhdhabtuhu)" when I attributed falsehood to him, even if I believed him to be truthful. And "I denied him" when I believed him to be lying, even if he was truthful. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿But if they deny you, then messengers before you were denied﴾, and He said: ﴿Indeed, they do not deny you﴾. The first means: if they attribute falsehood to you; the second means: they do not believe you to be a liar, but they deny the truth after knowing it, out of obstinacy and rejection. This is the root of this word. The verb transitively takes the object directly, and takes its report with the preposition "bi", and with negation. It is said "kadhdhabtuhu bi-kadhā" and "kadhdhabtuhu fihi"; the first is more common in usage. From it is His words: ﴿Rather, they denied the truth when it came to them﴾, and His words: ﴿And they denied Our signs﴾. Having understood this, [consider] His words: ﴿So what causes you to deny the Judgment after this?﴾

Scholars differ over (mā): is it in the sense of "what thing causes you to deny," or in the sense of "who is it that denies you"? Whoever takes it to mean "what thing" makes the address to the human being necessary, meaning: "What thing makes you, after this clarification, a denier of the religion, when the proofs of truth and of confirmation have become clear to you?" Whoever takes it to mean "who is it that denies you" makes the address to the Prophet. Al-Farra' said: it is as if he says, "Who can deny you concerning reward and punishment after what has been made clear to him of the creation of man as we have described?" Qatada said: "Who will deny you, O Messenger, after this, concerning the Judgment?"

According to the view of Qatada and al-Farra', there is a difficulty from two aspects:

The first: placing "mā" in the position of "man," and its matter is easy.

The second: the prepositional phrase requires an element it relates to, namely "yukadhdhibuka" (denies you), so that the meaning would be "who will make you a liar concerning the Judgment" or "who will make you one who denies it." Neither of these is valid. As for the second and third, it is evident: "kadhdhabtuhu" does not mean "I made him a liar" or "I made him one who denies," but rather "I attributed falsehood to him." So the meaning according to this would be "who will make you, after this, one who attributes falsehood concerning the Judgment?" And this is only transitive to its object by "bi" in the doubled verb, not the triliteral; one does not say "kadhaba kadhā" but rather "kadhaba bihi."

The answer to this difficulty is that the saying "kadhaba bi-kadhā" means: he declared the reported matter to be false; then the direct object was omitted because its knowledge is evident, so that it is as if it were forgotten. They made the verb transitive to the reported matter. Thus, when it is said "man yukadhdhibuka bi-kadhā," it means "they attribute falsehood to you concerning such-and-such," that is, they attribute falsehood to you in reporting it. Rather, the difficulty lies in the view of Mujahid and the majority: if the address is to the human being, and he is the one who denies (the doer of the denial), how can it be said to him "mā yukadhdhibuka," meaning "what makes you a denier"? The known usage is "kadhdhabahu" when he makes him a liar, not a denier; just as "fassaqahu" means he made him a sinner, not one who makes another a sinner.

The answer to this difficulty is that ṣaddaqa and kadhdhaba, in the doubled form, may carry two meanings. One is attribution, which applies to the object as you have mentioned. The other is the motive and impetus toward that act, which applies to the agent. Al-Kisa'i said: it is said "mā ṣaddaqaka bi-kadhā" or "mā kadhdhabaka bi-kadhā," meaning "what moved you to believe or to deny it?"

I say: this is parallel to "mā ajra'aka 'alā hādhā," meaning "what emboldened you to do this," and "mā qaddamaka wa-mā akhkharaka," meaning "what urged and moved you to advance or delay." This is a permissible usage, consistent with Arabic, and success is from God.

Then He concluded the surah with His words: ﴿Is not God the most just of judges?﴾ This is an affirmation of the content of the surah: the establishment of prophethood, monotheism, and the return; and His judgment includes His support for His Messenger against whoever denied him and rejected what he brought, through proof, power, and victory over him; and His judgment among His servants in this world through His law and command, and His judgment among them in the Hereafter through His reward and punishment. And the Most Just of judges does not befit the nullification of these judgments after His wisdom has been manifested in creating man in the best form and transferring him through stages of creation, state after state, to the most perfect condition. How then would it befit the Most Just of judges not to recompense the good-doer for his goodness and the wrongdoer for his wrongdoing? Would that not be a flaw in His judgment and His wisdom? So glory be to God, how concise is the wording of this surah, how great its significance, and how complete its meaning. And God knows best.
